grammar.title: Free indirect speech and the historic present
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Os três modos de representar pensamento:**
- **Discurso direto:** She thought, "**Why does** he always **do** this? **I'm** tired of it."
- **Discurso indireto:** She wondered **why he always did** that. She **was** tired of it.
- **Discurso indireto livre:** She looked at the clock. **Late again. Why did he always do this? Well, she was tired of it.**

**Características do discurso indireto livre:**
- **Terceira pessoa e passado** (como no indireto): "she was", "did he"
- **Sem verbo introdutório** ("she thought", "she wondered") — a mente da personagem entra direto na narração
- **Marcas da fala/pensamento da personagem:** perguntas, exclamações, interjeições, gírias, frases incompletas, dêiticos como **now, here, today, tomorrow** (em vez de then, there, the next day)
  - "Tomorrow she **would** tell him. **Yes**, tomorrow. **Enough** was enough!"
- **Efeito:** intimidade com a personagem **e** distância irônica ao mesmo tempo — o leitor nunca sabe se o julgamento é do narrador ou da personagem.

**2. O presente histórico** — narrar o passado no presente para criar **imediatismo**:
- Na fala informal: "So **I'm** at the bus stop, and this guy **comes** up to me and **says**..."
- Na ficção: "It **is** 1964. A woman **stands** at the window, waiting."
- Em manchetes e resumos de enredo: "In chapter 3, Capitu **meets** Bentinho..." (convenção para resumir obras!)

**3. Distância narrativa:**
- **Onisciente:** o narrador sabe tudo, entra em várias mentes.
- **Limitado:** segue uma personagem.
- **Não confiável:** o narrador distorce ou ignora a verdade (ex.: Bento Santiago em *Dom Casmurro*).

**4. Tempo verbal ao escrever sobre literatura:** use o **presente** ("literary present"): "Austen **uses** irony to..." / "The narrator **reveals**..."

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: Free indirect speech is so common in modern fiction that we hardly notice it. But it wasn't always there. Scholars often point to Jane Austen, writing in the early nineteenth century, as one of the first novelists in English to use it with real sophistication. In her novels, the narrator's voice slides almost imperceptibly into a character's thoughts — and back out again — so that we see the world through a character's eyes while also sensing the narrator's ironic distance. A century later, modernist writers like Virginia Woolf and James Joyce pushed the technique further, towards what's called stream of consciousness: the attempt to represent the flow of thought itself, with all its jumps, associations and fragments. In Brazilian literature, writers like Graciliano Ramos and Clarice Lispector explored similar territory. What all these writers share is a fascination with the gap between what people say and what they think — and the conviction that fiction is uniquely able to show us both.

reading.title: Whose voice is it?
reading.text: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." Few opening lines in English literature are as famous as the first sentence of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, published in 1813. Read quickly, it sounds like a solemn general statement. Read carefully, it is something far more slippery. Is it really a universal truth? Of course not. The sentence is ironic: what it describes is not a law of nature but the belief — or rather the hope — of the families with unmarried daughters who populate the novel. The next sentence confirms the joke: the "truth", we learn, is fixed in the minds of the neighbours, who regard any wealthy newcomer as "the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters". The real subject of the opening, then, is not rich men but the society that schemes to marry them. This ability to say one thing while meaning another — to adopt the voice of a character or a community while quietly mocking it — is at the heart of Austen's art, and it depends heavily on free indirect speech. Throughout the novel, the narrator moves in and out of characters' minds, especially that of the heroine, Elizabeth Bennet. We share her quick judgements and sharp observations, and we only gradually realize, as she does, how mistaken some of them are. The reader experiences prejudice from the inside before recognizing it from the outside. Two centuries later, the technique remains one of the most powerful tools available to novelists. It allows fiction to do something that no other art form can do so easily: to place us simultaneously inside and outside another person's mind. To read like a writer is, in large part, to learn to hear those two voices at once — and to ask, at every turn, whose voice we are really hearing.

writing.model:
The promotion

Renata arrived at the office forty minutes early, as she had every day for the past six years. The cleaning staff were still mopping the floors. Good. She liked the building like this: silent, orderly, waiting.

Today was the day. The director had called her in for a meeting at nine — "just a quick chat", he had said, which was exactly what people said when they didn't want to spoil a surprise. Who else could it be? Marcos was talented, of course, but he arrived at ten and left at six, and everyone knew he spent half the afternoon on his phone. No, it had to be her. Six years of early mornings. Six years of weekends answering emails. People noticed these things. They had to.

She made herself a coffee and sat down to review the quarterly figures one last time. Not that she needed to; she knew them by heart. But it never hurt to be prepared. Her mother had always said that luck was simply what happened when preparation met opportunity, and her mother had been right about most things, except perhaps about Renata's ex-husband.

At eight-thirty, Marcos walked in. Early, for once. He was wearing a new jacket — rather a nice one, actually — and he looked unusually pleased with himself.

"Morning, Renata! Big day today," he said, with a wink.

Big day? What did he mean by that? Surely he couldn't know about her meeting. Unless — no. The director would never discuss something like that with Marcos.

She smiled politely and returned to her spreadsheet. The numbers swam a little in front of her eyes. Well, it was early. She had slept badly. That was all.

At nine o'clock exactly, the director put his head round the door.

"Ah, both of you are here," he said. "Perfect. Marcos, would you come in first?"

grammar.title: Sound devices and rhythm
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Repetição de sons:**
- **Aliteração** — consoantes iniciais: "**P**eter **P**iper **p**icked...", "**b**ig **b**old **b**rands", "**c**ool, **c**alm and **c**ollected"
- **Assonância** — vogais: "the r**ai**n in Sp**ai**n st**ay**s m**ai**nly...", "h**ea**r the m**e**llow w**e**dding b**e**lls"
- **Consonância** — consoantes no meio/fim: "pi**tt**er-pa**tt**er", "bla**nk** and thi**nk**"
- **Rima** (final ou **interna**): "Once upon a midnight dr**eary**, while I pondered, weak and w**eary**" (Poe, 1845)

**2. Onomatopeia** — palavras que imitam sons: buzz, hiss, whisper, crash, murmur, sizzle, splash, thud, rustle, crackle, tick-tock
- Note que muitas são **verbos** em inglês: "The fire **crackled**." / "Leaves **rustled**."

**3. Ritmo acentual (stress-timed rhythm)**
- O inglês alterna sílabas **fortes** e **fracas**; as fortes caem em intervalos mais ou menos regulares e as fracas são **reduzidas** (schwa /ə/).
- "I **WANT** to **GO** to the **SHOPS**." (3 batidas) — "to the" quase some.
- Isso é muito diferente do português (mais "silábico"), e é uma das razões do sotaque estrangeiro.

**4. Métrica:**
- **Iambo** = fraca + **forte** (da-**DUM**): "be**LIEVE**", "to**DAY**"
- **Pentâmetro iâmbico** = 5 iambos por verso (10 sílabas) — o metro de Shakespeare:
  "Shall **I** com**PARE** thee **TO** a **SUM**mer's **DAY**?"
- **Troqueu** = **forte** + fraca (**DUM**-da): "**DOUB**le, **DOUB**le, **TOIL** and **TROU**ble" (*Macbeth*)

**5. Uso prático:** slogans ("**B**uy **b**etter, **b**uild **b**etter"), títulos ("*Pride and Prejudice*", "*Sense and Sensibility*"), marcas (Coca-Cola, Kit Kat), discursos e escrita criativa.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Why do children learn nursery rhymes so easily? Why do advertising jingles get stuck in our heads? Sound patterns like rhyme, rhythm and alliteration make language easier to process and to remember — which is why oral traditions all over the world, from ancient epic poetry to Brazilian cordel, relied on them long before writing was common. But there's a more surprising effect. In a study published in 2000, psychologists Matthew McGlone and Jessica Tofighbakhsh presented people with sayings in two versions: one that rhymed, like "Woes unite foes", and one that meant the same thing but didn't rhyme, like "Woes unite enemies". Participants judged the rhyming versions to be more accurate. Researchers sometimes call this the "rhyme-as-reason" effect. The sound of a statement, it seems, can influence whether we believe it. Which is a useful thing to know — both if you're writing a slogan, and if you're trying not to be fooled by one.

reading.title: Poetry for the ear
reading.text: For most of human history, poetry was something heard rather than read. Long before printed books, communities preserved their histories, laws and stories in verse, recited from memory by bards, griots and storytellers. Rhythm, rhyme and repetition were not decorations but tools: they made long texts easier to memorize and more pleasurable to hear. The Old English epic Beowulf, for instance, relies on heavy alliteration, each line typically linking two or three stressed words that begin with the same sound. Printing gradually changed the relationship between poetry and sound. As poems came to be read silently on the page, poets began to experiment with visual effects — line breaks, spacing, even the shape of the text. By the twentieth century, many poets had abandoned regular metre and rhyme altogether in favour of free verse, which follows the rhythms of natural speech rather than a fixed pattern. Some critics complained that poetry had lost its music, and with it much of its audience. In recent decades, however, the ear has made a remarkable comeback. Spoken word and slam poetry, performed live and shared online, have attracted a new generation of poets and listeners, many of whom would never have opened a poetry anthology. Hip-hop, with its intricate internal rhymes and rhythmic complexity, has been described by many critics as one of the most significant poetic forms of our time. In Brazil, repentistas improvising in verse, cordel writers and slam competitions in city squares have kept the oral tradition vividly alive. Perhaps the lesson is that poetry has never really stopped being music. Even the quietest poem on a page asks to be heard, if only in the reader's head. To read poetry well — in any language — is to listen as much as to look.

writing.model:
Rain in Belém, three o'clock

It begins, as it always begins, with a whisper.

A few fat drops tap on the tin roof of the market: tap, tap, tap, like a polite visitor. The vendors glance up, then down again. They know what's coming.

Then the sky splits. The rain rushes in, roaring on the roofs, drumming on the awnings, hammering the river until the whole city seems to hum. Gutters gurgle and overflow. Car tyres hiss through the flooded streets. A bus splashes past, and a woman shrieks, then laughs, her shopping bags soaked.

Under the mango trees, the world shrinks to a single sound — a steady, silver static, so loud it swallows every voice. Somewhere a radio crackles, fighting to be heard. A dog whimpers in a doorway. A child stamps in a puddle, delighted, defiant.

And then, as suddenly as it started, it stops.

Drip. Drip. Drip.

The leaves let go of the last of the water. The sun slides out from behind the clouds, and the steam rises softly from the warm, wet stones. The vendors shake their tarpaulins and shout their prices again. Birds begin, cautiously, to sing.

In Belém, they say you can set your watch by the rain. Three o'clock, every afternoon: the city's own symphony, played loud and short and true.

— Choices: onomatopoeia (tap, roaring, gurgle, hiss, splashes, shrieks, crackles, whimpers, drip) recreates the soundscape; alliteration (steady, silver static; delighted, defiant) and short sentences mimic the rhythm of the storm.

grammar.title: Punctuation for meaning and style
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Ponto e vírgula (;)** — liga **duas orações completas** relacionadas, sem conjunção:
- "It was late; everyone had gone home."
- Antes de advérbios conectivos: "The plan was risky; **however**, it worked."
- Em listas complexas com vírgulas internas: "We visited Recife, Pernambuco; Salvador, Bahia; and Natal, Rio Grande do Norte."

**2. Dois-pontos (:)** — **anuncia** o que vem: explicação, lista, citação, conclusão.
- "She had one goal: to win." / "The reason was simple: money."
- ⚠️ O que vem **antes** dos dois-pontos deve ser uma oração completa: ❌ "The ingredients are: eggs, flour..." ✅ "You need three ingredients: eggs, flour and milk."

**3. Travessão (—)** — interrupção, ênfase, reviravolta, aposto dramático:
- "He said yes — eventually."
- "Three people — my mother, my sister and a stranger — saw it happen."
- Mais informal e enfático que parênteses; em textos acadêmicos, use com moderação.

**4. Erros clássicos:**
- **Comma splice** (duas orações completas só com vírgula): ❌ "It was late, everyone had gone home." → use ponto, ponto e vírgula ou conjunção.
- ❌ "The plan was risky, however it worked." → "The plan was risky; however, it worked."
- **Run-on sentence:** duas orações sem nenhuma pontuação.

**5. Vírgula de Oxford** (antes do *and* final de uma lista) — opcional, mas evita ambiguidades:
- "I'd like to thank my parents, Ana**,** and God." (três grupos, não "meus pais, que são Ana e Deus")

**6. Variedade de frases (estilo):**
- **Frase cumulativa** — ideia principal no início, detalhes acumulados depois: "She walked into the sea, the water cold against her legs, the sun low over the horizon, the gulls crying above."
- **Frase periódica** — suspense, ideia principal **no fim**: "After years of struggle, countless rejections and one long, sleepless night, she finally said yes."
- **Fragmento intencional** — impacto: "He never came back. Never."
- **Regra de ouro:** alterne frases longas e curtas. Uma frase curta depois de várias longas **chama atenção**.

lines.speaker: Columnist
lines.en: Few punctuation marks inspire as much passion as the semicolon. Kurt Vonnegut famously advised writers not to use them at all, mocking them as pretentious — before, with typical irony, using one himself a few pages later. Other writers adore them. To their fans, the semicolon is the most elegant mark in the language: stronger than a comma, gentler than a full stop, it joins two ideas that belong together without forcing them into a single sentence. The truth, as usual, lies somewhere in between. Overused, semicolons can make writing feel heavy and academic. Used well, they create subtle connections that no other mark can manage. My advice? Before you use one, ask yourself a simple question: could each side stand alone as a sentence? If not, it's the wrong mark. And if yes — ask whether the two ideas are close enough to share a breath. If they are, go ahead. If not, a full stop will do the job; it usually does.

reading.title: The rhythm of prose
reading.text: Writers have long understood that prose, like music, has rhythm, and that rhythm depends not only on words but on the shape of sentences. In a much-quoted passage from his book The Way We Write, the American writing teacher Gary Provost demonstrated this with a simple experiment. He wrote a paragraph composed entirely of five-word sentences. It was grammatically perfect. It was also, as he pointed out, monotonous. Then he varied the length: a short sentence, a medium one, and then a long, rolling sentence that built and built until it reached its climax. The second version, he argued, did not merely inform; it sang. The lesson is easily overlooked by learners, who often focus on accuracy at the expense of rhythm. A text made entirely of short sentences can sound childish or breathless. A text made entirely of long, complex sentences can exhaust the reader, however impressive each individual sentence may be. The most effective writers alternate. They use long, cumulative sentences to describe and accumulate detail, allowing the reader to settle into a scene; they use periodic sentences, which delay the main point until the end, to build suspense; and they use short sentences — sometimes no more than a word or two — for emphasis, surprise or finality. Punctuation is the instrument that makes this possible. The comma lets a sentence breathe. The semicolon holds two ideas in balance. The colon creates expectation: something important is coming. The dash interrupts, adds, surprises. And the full stop, the most underestimated of all, gives the reader a moment of silence in which a sentence can resonate. None of this can be learned from rules alone. It must be heard. Reading good prose aloud, slowly, remains one of the best ways to develop an ear for rhythm. So does reading your own writing aloud. If you run out of breath, the sentence is too long. If it sounds like a list, it probably needs a variation. Try it.

questions.q: What did Gary Provost's experiment show?
questions.answer: Sentences of the same length are monotonous; varying length creates rhythm.

questions.q: What are cumulative sentences good for?
questions.answer: Describing and accumulating detail.

questions.q: What are periodic sentences good for?
questions.answer: Building suspense by delaying the main point.

questions.q: What practical advice does the text give?
questions.answer: Read good prose and your own writing aloud to develop an ear for rhythm.

The phone call

I was nineteen when the phone rang at three in the morning. Nobody calls at three in the morning with good news; I knew that even before I picked it up.

It was my uncle. His voice was strange — flat, careful, as if each word had been chosen in advance. My father had been taken to hospital. A heart attack. They didn't know yet.

I remember very little of the drive. I remember the empty avenues, the traffic lights changing for nobody, the orange glow of the streetlamps sliding across the windscreen, my mother's hand gripping the door handle so tightly that her knuckles were white. I remember thinking one thing over and over: not yet.

The hospital was too bright. Everything in it was too bright: the floors, the walls, the forced smiles of the nurses who told us to wait. So we waited. We waited for four hours; it felt like four days.

And then, after a night of silence, after the coffee from the machine and the prayers I didn't know I remembered, after watching every door open and close and open again, a young doctor walked towards us and smiled.

He was going to be fine.

My father lived for another twenty-two years. He became, if anything, more stubborn after that night — he refused to give up salt, coffee or football — but he also became softer in ways I hadn't expected. He started telling us he loved us. Often. Sometimes too often, my sister used to joke.

I still think about that drive whenever my phone rings at night. Fear, I learned, is not the opposite of love; it is one of its shapes. And gratitude, when it finally comes, arrives quietly: a doctor's smile, a corridor, a door that opens the right way.

grammar.title: Evaluative language and review structure
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Vocabulário avaliativo preciso** — substitua "good / bad / interesting":
- **Positivo:** accomplished, assured, compelling, luminous, nuanced, haunting, exhilarating, beautifully observed, a tour de force
- **Negativo:** derivative, formulaic, self-indulgent, overwrought, heavy-handed, laboured, uneven, patchy, forgettable
- **Neutro/descritivo:** understated, ambitious, sprawling, experimental, slow-paced, unconventional

**2. Avaliação com nuance** — o crítico C2 raramente é totalmente positivo ou negativo:
- **if / albeit** concessivo: "an **accomplished, if uneven**, debut" / "a **powerful, albeit flawed**, film"
- **never quite / not entirely / falls short of**: "The ending **never quite** convinces." / "It **falls short of** its ambitions."
- **what it lacks in X, it makes up for in Y**: "**What it lacks in** originality, **it makes up for in** charm."
- **for all its flaws / for all its brilliance** (apesar de): "**For all its flaws**, it's a remarkable achievement."
- **the film / book is at its best when...**: "The novel **is at its best when** it focuses on the family."

**3. Estrutura de uma review C2 (280–320 palavras):**
1. **Abertura com gancho + contexto** (autor/diretor, gênero, expectativa)
2. **Resumo breve** (sem spoilers!), no **presente**
3. **Análise** de 2–3 aspectos (atuação, roteiro, estilo, temas) com exemplos
4. **Pontos fracos** com nuance
5. **Avaliação final + recomendação** (para quem?)

**4. Registro:** semiformal, com personalidade; pode usar humor e opinião pessoal, mas sempre **justificada**.

listening.title: What makes a good critic?
listening.context_pt: Uma editora de cultura de um jornal fala sobre o papel da crítica.

lines.speaker: Editor
lines.en: People sometimes assume that a critic's job is simply to tell you whether something is good or bad. That's the least interesting part of it. A good critic does three things. First, they describe the work vividly enough that you can imagine it, without giving away what shouldn't be given away. Second, they analyse — they explain how the work achieves its effects, or why it fails to. And third, they place it in context: what is this artist trying to do, how does it relate to their earlier work, or to the tradition it belongs to? The verdict comes last, and it should feel earned. The worst reviews, in my experience, are the ones that are either entirely gushing or entirely dismissive. Real works of art are rarely perfect or worthless. Even a masterpiece has weaknesses; even a failure may contain moments of genuine brilliance. A critic's real value lies in noticing both — and in helping readers see what they might otherwise have missed.

questions.q: Where does a critic's real value lie?

reading.title: Review: The House of the Two Rivers
reading.text:
(The novel reviewed below is fictional and was created for this lesson.)

Few debut novels arrive with as much expectation as The House of the Two Rivers, the first book by the Manaus-born writer Helena Barros. Shortlisted for a major prize before its publication in English, it has been described by its publishers as "the great Amazonian family saga". It is not quite that — but it is something more interesting.

The novel follows three generations of the Andrade family, rubber merchants whose fortunes rise and fall with the boom and collapse of the trade in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. At its centre is the family's crumbling mansion, built where two rivers meet, and Dona Clara, the formidable matriarch who refuses to leave it even as the city around her decays.

Barros is at her best when she slows down. Her descriptions of the river at dawn, of the humid stillness of the house in the afternoon, of the small rituals of a family pretending nothing has changed, are luminous. Her prose is understated yet precise, and her use of free indirect speech allows us to inhabit Clara's mind while quietly exposing her illusions. The scenes between Clara and her granddaughter, in particular, are a masterclass in what goes unsaid.

The novel is less assured when it tries to cover too much ground. A subplot involving a foreign engineer feels heavy-handed, and the final section, which jumps abruptly to the 1970s, reads more like an epilogue than a conclusion. At over five hundred pages, the book occasionally sags, and a firmer editorial hand might have produced a tighter, more powerful novel.

For all its flaws, however, this is an accomplished and haunting debut. What it lacks in structural discipline, it more than makes up for in atmosphere, emotional intelligence and sheer beauty of language. Readers who enjoy slow, immersive fiction will find much to admire. Barros is a writer to watch; her second novel may well be a masterpiece.

questions.answer: It's not quite "the great Amazonian family saga" — but something more interesting.

questions.q: When is the writer "at her best"?
questions.answer: When she slows down — in descriptions and quiet family scenes.

questions.q: What weaknesses does the reviewer identify?
questions.answer: A heavy-handed subplot, an abrupt final section, and occasional sagging due to length.

questions.q: Who does the reviewer recommend the novel to?
questions.answer: Readers who enjoy slow, immersive fiction.

writing.model:
Vidas Secas (Barren Lives), by Graciliano Ramos

Few novels manage to say so much in so few pages. First published in 1938 and available in English as Barren Lives, Graciliano Ramos's portrait of a family of migrants fleeing drought in the Brazilian sertão is barely 150 pages long, yet it remains one of the most powerful works of Brazilian literature.

The novel follows Fabiano, his wife Sinha Vitória, their two sons and their dog, Baleia, as they wander across the parched landscape of the Northeast in search of work and water. Very little happens, in the conventional sense. The family finds shelter on an abandoned farm, endures the cruelty of a landowner and a soldier, and is eventually forced to move on again.

What makes the book extraordinary is its form. Each chapter focuses on a different character, and Ramos uses free indirect speech to enter minds that have almost no words of their own. Fabiano struggles to express his anger; the children ask questions nobody can answer; and in the most famous chapter, the narrative enters the consciousness of the dying dog with a tenderness that is almost unbearable. Ramos's prose is spare, precise and utterly unsentimental — as dry, one might say, as the landscape it describes.

The novel is not without its challenges for international readers. Its episodic structure can feel fragmentary, and some cultural and historical references may be unfamiliar without a good introduction. Its bleakness, too, will not be to everyone's taste.

For all that, it is a masterpiece that has stood the test of time remarkably well. In an age of climate migration and growing inequality, its portrait of people driven from their land by forces beyond their control feels anything but dated. Readers who admire the restraint of writers such as Steinbeck or Coetzee will find in Ramos a kindred spirit — and a voice the world should hear far more often.

Rating: ★★★★★
